rule: If the mouth looks off, compare with the reference to decide whether to move it up or down, make it smaller or larger, or change the values such as a darker top lip or a larger bottom lip.
Light the model from an angle rather than straight on; straight-on lighting makes the image look flat and hides the planes and contours of the form.
When lighting is too even from both sides it can cause a shadow that divides the model in half.
In the three-quarter view from below, the guidelines for the mouth, nose and eyes are not straight but tilted at about 15 degrees.
Shadows are not just one tone but vary in lightness and darkness; subtle changes in shadow values create depth.
The area right under the chin is much darker than the middle section of the neck.
Do not just create one big black shape for an open mouth; draw in the teeth and tongue to add energy to the expression.
Never draw a face from a memorized pattern of an oval, dividing lines, almond eyes and a triangle nose, because it will not work from different angles.
